angle: psychology of people who grew up then
title: The Psychology of People Who Grew Up in the 1950s (It's Not What You Think)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, yesterday you laughed at me. You opened my kitchen drawer and found forty rubber bands, a hundred twist ties, and a stack of margarine tubs I've washed and saved. And you said, Grandma, why do you keep all this? And I laughed too. But then I thought about it all night. Because there's a reason. There's a reason for almost everything people like me do.
scenes.caption: WHY DO YOU KEEP ALL THIS?

scenes.text: People who grew up in the nineteen fifties are a little strange to you. We say things you don't understand. We do things that drive your mother crazy. So tonight, I'm going to explain us. Eleven things about how we think, and exactly where each one came from. And maybe next time you'll laugh a little less. Maybe.
scenes.query: 1950s family portrait living room parents children
scenes.caption: ELEVEN THINGS

scenes.text: Number one. We waste nothing. Not a crust, not a rubber band, not a piece of string. And that didn't start with us, honey. It started with our parents and grandparents, who lived through the Great Depression. Grandma Pearl stood in a bread line in Mansfield in nineteen thirty-two. She raised two boys on almost nothing. And she raised my mother to be the same way, and my mother raised me.
scenes.caption: THE BREAD LINE

scenes.text: In our house, bacon grease went into a can on the stove for cooking. Old shirts became dish rags, then floor rags. Bread heels went into bread pudding. Grandma Pearl used to say, use it up, wear it out, make it do, or do without. Every child of the fifties heard those words. That's why I save the margarine tubs. Some part of me still thinks the Depression could come back on Tuesday.
scenes.caption: USE IT UP, WEAR IT OUT

scenes.text: We ate everything on our plates, too. My mother would say, there are children starving in Europe, and I would say, then send them my lima beans. That got me sent to my room. Leftovers became Monday's soup. Sour milk became pancakes. To this day, honey, I cannot scrape food into the garbage without feeling a little pinch in my chest. It feels like a sin.
scenes.caption: CLEAN YOUR PLATE

scenes.text: Number two. We fix things. When the toaster broke, my father took it apart on the kitchen table and fixed it with a screwdriver. When my shoe sole came loose, we took it to the shoe repair man for a quarter. When the television went dark, a man came to the house with a box of tubes. Nobody threw anything away just because it broke. You fixed it. That was the whole point of owning it.
scenes.query: 1950s man repairing toaster kitchen table tools
scenes.caption: WITH A SCREWDRIVER

scenes.text: So when you tell me to just buy a new one, sweetheart, I hear my father's voice saying, what's wrong with this one? And honestly, half the time, nothing is wrong with it. It just needs a screw tightened. Try it sometime. Fix one thing yourself this month. You'll feel ten feet tall.
scenes.caption: WHAT'S WRONG WITH THIS ONE?

scenes.text: Number three. We are afraid of debt. In my family, if you couldn't pay cash for it, you didn't buy it. My father bought our house with a mortgage from the GI Bill, after the war, and he paid it off five years early and threw a party. Our first car, our first television, our first refrigerator. All cash. My father said, a man who owes money doesn't own his own life.
scenes.query: 1950s couple new house front door GI Bill
scenes.caption: PAID IT OFF EARLY

scenes.text: The first credit card came out in nineteen fifty, the Diners Club, for restaurants. Then BankAmericard in nineteen fifty-eight. My father would never have one. He paid for everything in cash, from an envelope in his dresser, until the day he died. I have one card now, sweetheart, and I pay it off every month. If I didn't, I'd hear him in my sleep.
scenes.query: 1950s man paying cash wallet store counter
scenes.caption: AN ENVELOPE IN HIS DRESSER

scenes.text: Number four. We don't complain. Or we try not to. When you scraped your knee, my mother said, you'll live. When you were sad, she said, chin up. When you were bored, she said, only boring people get bored, go outside. Nobody asked how we felt about things. Our fathers had come home from a war, and they didn't talk about how they felt. So neither did we.
scenes.caption: CHIN UP

scenes.text: I won't pretend that was all good, honey. A lot of people from my time carried things inside them their whole lives and never said a word. Men who drank too much. Women who were sad behind the kitchen door. Your generation talks about feelings, and I think that's better. I really do. But we got through a great deal, keeping our chins up.
scenes.caption: BEHIND THE KITCHEN DOOR

scenes.text: Number five. We know how to wait. Everything took time. You ordered from the Sears catalog and waited three weeks. You sent a letter and waited a week for an answer. Your favorite television show was on once a week, Tuesday night at eight, and if you missed it, you missed it. Forever. There was no rewinding. You waited for Christmas for a whole year. And the waiting was half the fun.
scenes.caption: THREE WEEKS

scenes.text: Long distance telephone calls were for emergencies only. If the phone rang after nine at night, my mother's face went white, because it meant somebody had died. When Grandma Pearl called from Columbus, my father stood next to the phone watching the clock, saying, Ma, this is costing a dollar a minute. So we wrote letters instead. Every week. Pages and pages.
scenes.caption: A DOLLAR A MINUTE

scenes.text: So when you can't wait four seconds for a video to load, sweetheart, I have to smile. I once waited six months for a pen pal in France to write back. Her name was Monique. When her letter came, I read it forty times. You don't read anything forty times anymore. Maybe you should try it with something that matters.
scenes.caption: MONIQUE

scenes.text: Number six. We are formal. Every grownup was Mister or Missus. Mrs. Pruitt, Mr. Hoffman, Dr. Hartman. You would no more call a grownup by their first name than fly to the moon. You said yes ma'am and no sir. You stood up when an older person came into the room. And you wrote a thank-you note for every single present, by hand, before New Year's, or you didn't get to play with it.
scenes.query: 1950s child writing thank you note desk
scenes.caption: THANK-YOU NOTES

scenes.text: And when the telephone rang, you answered it, Miller residence, Ruth speaking. Every child knew to say that. Your mother laughs when I still answer that way sometimes. But it meant something, honey. It meant that you belonged to a house, and a family, and that how you behaved was a reflection on all of them.
scenes.caption: MILLER RESIDENCE

scenes.text: Number seven. We think children can take care of themselves. Because we did. At nine I walked downtown alone. At ten I took Danny to the movies on the bus. We left in the morning and came home when the streetlights came on, and nobody knew where we were. We fell out of trees, we got lost, we got into trouble, and we got ourselves out of it.
scenes.caption: HOME WHEN THE LIGHTS CAME ON

scenes.text: So when I see your mother tracking you on her phone, I understand it. The world feels more dangerous now. But I also think, she'll be fine. Let her get a little lost. That's how you learn the way home. Sweetheart, getting lost was the best thing that ever happened to me.
scenes.query: 1950s girl riding bicycle country road alone
scenes.caption: LET HER GET A LITTLE LOST

scenes.text: Number eight. We stay. My father worked at the Westinghouse plant for thirty-one years. He got a gold watch. Your grandfather worked at one place for most of his life. We stayed married, even when it was hard. We went to the same church, the same grocery store, the same barber, for forty years. Loyalty was the most important thing a person could have.
scenes.caption: THIRTY-ONE YEARS

scenes.text: Sometimes that was foolish, honey. Some people stayed in jobs that ground them down, and in marriages that should have ended. But there was something good in it too. When you stay somewhere for forty years, everybody knows your name. When my father died, three hundred people came to his funeral. Three hundred. I don't think that happens much anymore.
scenes.caption: THREE HUNDRED PEOPLE

scenes.text: Number nine. We dress up. My mother wore a hat and gloves to go downtown. My father wore a tie to the doctor. People wore their Sunday best to fly on an airplane, sweetheart, and to go to the movies. You dressed up because it showed respect. For the place, and for the people there. Coming to the grocery store in your pajamas would have been the scandal of the year.
scenes.caption: OUR SUNDAY BEST

scenes.text: I still can't go to the doctor in a sweatshirt, sweetheart. I put on a blouse and my good earrings, every time. Your mother says, Mom, it's just a checkup. But my mother's voice is in my head, saying, you never know who you'll meet, Ruth Ann. And she was right, you know. I met your grandfather at a church social in nineteen sixty-three, wearing my best blue dress and white gloves. If I'd been wearing a sweatshirt, you might not be here.
scenes.caption: MY BEST BLUE DRESS

scenes.text: Number ten. We grew up afraid, and it made us tough. Of polio, every summer. Of the atomic bomb. We crawled under our desks at school and practiced hiding from the end of the world. In October of nineteen sixty-two, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, I truly thought I'd never turn nineteen. And then we got up and went to school anyway. You learn something from that. You learn that you keep going.
scenes.query: 1950s school duck and cover drill children desks
scenes.caption: WE KEPT GOING

scenes.text: Every summer there was polio. Swimming pools closed. Mothers kept children inside in August. A boy in my class, Richard Hale, went to the hospital in nineteen fifty-two and came back in leg braces. Then in April of nineteen fifty-five they announced the Salk vaccine worked, and the church bells rang all over Mansfield. We lined up at school for our shots, and nobody cried. Not one child. We knew what it meant.
scenes.query: 1950s children polio vaccine line school nurse
scenes.caption: NOBODY CRIED

scenes.text: And number eleven. We believed things would get better. That's the biggest one, sweetheart. Our parents had lived through the Depression and the war, and after that, every year was better than the last. A new car, a new house, a television, a vacation. We truly believed that our children would have more than we did. That if you worked hard and played fair, it would work out.
scenes.query: 1950s happy family new car suburban driveway
scenes.caption: EVERY YEAR WAS BETTER

scenes.text: Not everyone got that promise, I know. Not everybody in America in the fifties was allowed to have it. But in our little house on Elm Street, we believed it. And I still do, a little. Even now. That's why I save the margarine tubs, honey. Not because I think things will get worse. Because I always thought they'd get better, and somebody might need a margarine tub.
scenes.caption: SOMEBODY MIGHT NEED IT

scenes.text: So now you know us a little better. We waste nothing, we fix things, we hate debt, we don't complain, we know how to wait, we say thank you, we let children roam, we stay, we dress up, we keep going, and we believe. Tell me in the comments which one is you, or your mother, or your grandfather. I'll bet it's more than one. Goodnight, sweetheart. Grandma Ruth will be right here tomorrow.
scenes.caption: WHICH ONE IS YOU?
